passages.happening:
Jesus stays in Galilee. He does not want to go about in Judea, because ‘the Jews there’ are trying to kill him (verse 1). But the Feast of Tabernacles is near.

His brothers push him. “Leave here and go to Judea, so that Your disciples there may see the works You are doing” (verse 3). No one who wants to be known works in secret, they say. Show yourself to the world. John adds a quiet, painful line: “For even His own brothers did not believe in Him” (verse 5).

Jesus answers that his time has not yet come, while their time is always ready. The world cannot hate them, but it hates him, because he says its works are evil. “Go up to the feast on your own. I am not going up to this feast, because My time has not yet come” (verse 8). And he stays in Galilee.
passages.hearers:
‘The Jews there’ in verse 1 are the leaders in Judea and Jerusalem who wanted Jesus dead after chapter 5, not the Jewish people. Jesus, his brothers and his disciples are all Jews, on their way to a Jewish feast. John's book page explains the phrase in its part on ‘the Jews’ in John.

Tabernacles, also called Booths, was a great autumn feast. Pilgrims came to Jerusalem from all over the land. Families lived for a week in shelters made of branches, to remember the years Israel lived in tents in the wilderness. It was also a harvest festival, full of joy.

His brothers' advice sounds like good sense. A feast in Jerusalem was the biggest stage in the land. If you want followers, go where the crowds are. But John tells us why they said it: they did not believe in him. Who these brothers were, whether sons of Mary and Joseph, sons of Joseph from an earlier marriage, or cousins, Christians answer differently; the note on Mark 3:20-35 sets out the three readings. What matters here is that his own family did not yet believe.

And yet the story did not end there. After the resurrection, Jesus' brothers are among the believers praying in Jerusalem (Acts 1:14). The risen Jesus appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), and Paul later calls him ‘James, the Lord's brother’ (Galatians 1:19), a leader of the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13).
passages.ot: The feast was commanded in the Law: “You are to dwell in booths for seven days” (Leviticus 23:42), “so that your descendants may know that I made the Israelites dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt” (Leviticus 23:43). It was a feast of joy: “And you shall rejoice in your feast” (Deuteronomy 16:14). Every seventh year, Moses commanded, the Law was to be read aloud to all Israel at this feast (Deuteronomy 31:10-11).
passages.hard:
Did Jesus mislead his brothers? He says, ‘I am not going up to this feast’ (verse 8), and then, in verse 10, he goes. This was noticed very early, and critics of Christianity have used it to accuse Jesus of changing his mind.

Some early copies of John, including the papyri P66 and P75 and Codex Vaticanus, read ‘I am not yet going up’. Most scholars think a scribe wrote ‘yet’ to ease the difficulty, though a few think ‘not yet’ is original. Many who accept ‘not’ point to Jesus' own reason: ‘My time has not yet come.’ He would not go up on his brothers' terms, as a public show to win a following. He went later, quietly, in his own time. Others note that in John ‘going up’ can also mean going up to the Father (20:17), and that time had not yet come. All these readings agree on what the scene shows: Jesus would not let anyone else set his timetable, not even his family.
passages.asks: It is a lonely thing when your own family does not share your faith, or mocks it. Jesus knew that from the inside. He did not argue his brothers into belief, and he did not cut them off. Some of them came to faith later. If you are praying for family members who do not believe, this chapter gives you no promise of a timetable, but it does give you hope.

passages.happening:
After his brothers have gone, Jesus goes up too, ‘not publicly, but in secret’ (verse 10).

At the feast the leaders are looking for him: “Where is He?” (verse 11). The crowds whisper about him. Some say, “He is a good man.” Others say, “No, He deceives the people” (verse 12). “Yet no one would speak publicly about Him for fear of the Jews” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Verse 13 shows clearly what John means by ‘the Jews’ in such places. The people who are afraid are Jews themselves, Jewish pilgrims at a Jewish feast. They are afraid of ‘the Jews’. So the phrase cannot mean the Jewish people. It means the authorities in Jerusalem, the people with power to punish. John uses it the same way later, when the parents of the man born blind are ‘afraid of the Jews’ (9:22), and when the disciples lock their doors ‘for fear of the Jews’ (20:19), though all of them are Jews.

Two verdicts run through the crowd: a good man, or a deceiver. The second was a serious charge. The Law warned against prophets who led people astray from God. To call Jesus a deceiver was to say he was dangerous.
passages.ot: The Law of Moses gave Israel a strong warning against anyone who would lead the people away from the LORD (Deuteronomy 13:1-5). That is the background of the whispered charge, ‘He deceives the people’. The crowd is asking a real question that Scripture itself had taught them to ask: is this man from God, or is he leading us astray?
passages.asks: Many people today hold an opinion about Jesus but keep it quiet, afraid of what others will say. Some fear religious people; some fear people who mock religion. John names that fear without scorn. But he also shows, through the whole book, people who stop whispering and speak.

passages.happening:
Halfway through the feast, Jesus goes up into the temple courts and begins to teach. The leaders are amazed: “How did this man attain such learning without having studied?” (verse 15).

“My teaching is not My own,” Jesus answers. “It comes from Him who sent Me” (verse 16). Anyone who truly wants to do God's will, he says, will know whether his teaching is from God. Then he goes on the attack. Moses gave you the law, yet none of you keeps it. “Why are you trying to kill Me?” “You have a demon,” the crowd answers. “Who is trying to kill You?” (verse 20).

Jesus reminds them of the healing at the pool in chapter 5. They circumcise a baby boy on the Sabbath so as not to break the law of Moses. “Why are you angry with Me for making the whole man well on the Sabbath?” (verse 23). “Stop judging by outward appearances, and start judging justly” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
‘Without having studied’ means Jesus had not trained under a known teacher. A teacher's authority usually came from the teacher he had studied under. Later the council will be just as surprised that Peter and John are ‘unschooled, ordinary men’ (Acts 4:13). Jesus says he has a teacher: the one who sent him.

The crowd's ‘Who is trying to kill You?’ shows that many pilgrims did not know what the leaders were planning. ‘The crowd’ and ‘the Jews’ in this chapter are different groups.

The argument about circumcision used a rule the hearers already accepted. The Law said a boy was to be circumcised on the eighth day. If the eighth day fell on a Sabbath, the circumcision was done anyway. The Mishnah, a book of Jewish teaching written down around AD 200, sets out this rule: circumcision on the eighth day overrides the Sabbath (Shabbat 19). It is later than Jesus, but the custom it records was clearly known, since Jesus can take it for granted. His point: if you may perform a rite on one part of a boy's body on the Sabbath, how can it be wrong to make a whole man well?
passages.ot: The Law commanded, “on the eighth day the flesh of the boy's foreskin is to be circumcised” (Leviticus 12:3). Jesus adds that it came first ‘from the patriarchs’, since God gave it to Abraham before Moses (Genesis 17:12). And his call to judge justly echoes Moses' charge to Israel's judges: “Show no partiality in judging; hear both small and great alike” (Deuteronomy 1:17). Isaiah said the promised king “will not judge by what His eyes see” (Isaiah 11:3).
passages.hard:
Does verse 17 mean that anyone who does not believe in Jesus must be unwilling to obey God? It is better read as an invitation than an accusation. Jesus says that a person who truly wants to do God's will is in a position to recognize whether his teaching is from God. It does not say every doubter is dishonest. Many people have honest doubts. The verse asks them to begin with willingness: if this is from God, I want to do it.

And does ‘stop judging by outward appearances’ forbid all moral judgment? No. The same sentence says ‘start judging justly’. Jesus does not say ‘do not judge’. He says judge rightly, by what is true and not by what is on the surface.
passages.asks: Jesus invites a test anyone can try: want to do God's will, and see whether his teaching rings true. You do not need to settle every question first. You need a willing heart. That is open to a skeptic as much as to a believer.

passages.t: Where is he from, and where is he going?
passages.happening:
Some of the people of Jerusalem start talking. Isn't this the man they want to kill? Yet here he is, speaking openly, and no one stops him. Have the rulers decided he is the Christ? “But we know where this man is from. When the Christ comes, no one will know where He is from” (verse 27).

Jesus cries out in the temple courts, “You know Me, and you know where I am from. I have not come of My own accord, but He who sent Me is true. You do not know Him, but I know Him, because I am from Him and He sent Me” (verses 28-29).

They try to seize him, but no one lays a hand on him, because his hour has not yet come. Many in the crowd believe in him. The Pharisees and chief priests send officers to arrest him. Jesus says, “I am with you only a little while longer, and then I am going to the One who sent Me” (verse 33). You will look for me and not find me. The leaders are puzzled. Will he go to the Jews scattered among the Greeks, and teach the Greeks?
passages.hearers:
Some Jews of that time believed the Messiah would be hidden until the moment he appeared. In the second century the Christian writer Justin Martyr, in his Dialogue with Trypho, has a Jewish man named Trypho say that the Christ, if already born, is unknown, and has no power until Elijah comes to anoint him and make him known (Dialogue 8). That book is later than John, but it shows a hope like the one in verse 27. The people of Jerusalem think: we know this man's family and his town; the real Messiah will come out of nowhere.

John lets the irony stand. They think they know where Jesus is from: Nazareth in Galilee. Jesus says they do not know where he is really from. He is from the Father.

‘The Jews dispersed among the Greeks’ (verse 35) were the many Jewish communities living outside the land, in Greek-speaking cities across the Roman world. The leaders mean it as a sneer: will he go off and teach foreigners? John's readers would smile. That is just what happened. After the resurrection, the message about Jesus went out to the Greeks, and John's own Gospel was written in Greek.
passages.ot: The promise of a ruler from Bethlehem is in Micah: “But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come forth for Me One to be ruler over Israel” (Micah 5:2). The same verse goes on to say that his origins are ‘of old, from the days of eternity’. So the prophets had already hinted at what Jesus says here: the Messiah has a family and a hometown, and also an origin far older than either.
passages.asks: The people of Jerusalem thought they had Jesus figured out because they knew his background. It is easy to dismiss someone because we think we know where they come from. Jesus asks his hearers, and us, to look further: not only where he grew up, but who sent him.

passages.happening:
“On the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood up and called out in a loud voice, ‘If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink. Whoever believes in Me, as the Scripture has said: ‘Streams of living water will flow from within him.’’” (verses 37-38).

John explains: “He was speaking about the Spirit, whom those who believed in Him were later to receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (verse 39).
passages.hearers:
Picture the setting. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, describes a ceremony at this feast. Each morning a priest carried water from the pool of Siloam up to the temple and poured it out at the altar, with great rejoicing. At night great lamps lit the Court of the Women. The Mishnah even says that whoever had not seen the rejoicing at the water-drawing had never seen rejoicing in his life (Sukkah 5:1). How much of this was already done in Jesus' day is not certain, as John's book page says. But if it was, Jesus stood up on the last day of a feast full of water and light and cried out: if anyone is thirsty, come to me. A few verses later he will say, ‘I am the light of the world’ (8:12).

Tabernacles came at the end of the dry summer, just before the rains. A prayer for water was a prayer for life for the coming year.

Verse 39 has a striking phrase. The Greek says literally, ‘for the Spirit was not yet’, and translators add ‘given’. John does not mean the Spirit did not exist; the Spirit is in the Old Testament from its first page. He means the Spirit had not yet been poured out on believers as Jesus promised. That would come after Jesus was ‘glorified’, which in John means lifted up on the cross and raised to the Father. Jesus breathes the Spirit on his disciples after the resurrection (20:22), and Peter says at Pentecost that the risen Jesus has poured out the Spirit (Acts 2:33).
passages.ot: No single verse matches ‘Streams of living water will flow from within him’ word for word. Readers point to several passages that may lie behind it. Zechariah: “on that day living water will flow out from Jerusalem” (Zechariah 14:8), in a chapter where the nations come “to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles” (Zechariah 14:16). Ezekiel's river: “I saw water flowing from under the threshold of the temple” (Ezekiel 47:1). Isaiah: “You will be like a well-watered garden, like a spring whose waters never fail” (Isaiah 58:11), and “With joy you will draw water from the springs of salvation” (Isaiah 12:3). And the rock in the wilderness: “He brought streams from the stone and made water flow down like rivers” (Psalm 78:16; Exodus 17:6). Jesus may be gathering several of these into one promise.
passages.hard:
Whose heart do the streams flow from? The oldest Greek copies had no punctuation, so the sentence can be divided two ways.

In the reading most Bibles follow, including the Berean Standard Bible, the streams flow from within the believer. The one who comes to Jesus and drinks becomes a source of life for others.

In the other reading, verse 37 ends ‘let him come to Me and drink, whoever believes in Me’. Then the words ‘from within him’ point to Jesus himself. He is the source. Readers who prefer this point to Ezekiel's river flowing from the temple, and to John's own words that Jesus' body is the true temple (2:21). They also remember that at the cross ‘blood and water flowed out’ from Jesus' side (19:34).

Early Christian teachers already read the verse both ways, and both readings agree that the water is the Spirit and that Jesus is the one who gives it. These notes do not choose.
passages.asks: Jesus' invitation has one condition: thirst. Not goodness, not knowledge, not a tidy life. If you feel dry, empty, or worn out, with nothing left to give, you are exactly the kind of person he called out to. Come and drink.

passages.happening:
The crowd is split. Some say, “This is truly the Prophet” (verse 40). Others say, “This is the Christ.” Still others answer, “How can the Christ come from Galilee? Doesn't the Scripture say that the Christ will come from the line of David and from Bethlehem, the village where David lived?” (verses 41-42).

“So there was division in the crowd because of Jesus” (verse 43). Some want to seize him, but no one lays a hand on him.
passages.hearers:
The crowd's objection was a fair one. They knew their Scriptures. The Messiah was to be a son of David, and Micah named Bethlehem. Jesus was known as a man from Nazareth in Galilee.

John does not stop to correct them. Matthew and Luke both say Jesus was born in Bethlehem and was of David's line (Matthew 2:1; Luke 2:4). Many readers think John knew this and expects his readers to know it too. The crowd is sure Jesus cannot be the Christ because he comes from Galilee, when in fact he was born in Bethlehem, and more deeply, comes from the Father. John uses this kind of irony often. Other scholars think John was not interested in Jesus' birthplace, only in his coming from God. John's text itself does not settle which.

Notice the word ‘division’. Jesus divides people, not because he wants quarrels, but because no one can stay neutral about him for long.
passages.ot: God promised David, “I will raise up your descendant after you, who will come from your own body, and I will establish his kingdom” (2 Samuel 7:12). And Micah named the town, Bethlehem: “out of you will come forth for Me One to be ruler over Israel” (Micah 5:2). Yet Isaiah also gave Galilee a promise: in the future God “will honor the Way of the Sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations” (Isaiah 9:1). Matthew quotes that very passage about Jesus beginning his work in Galilee.
passages.asks: The crowd argued about Jesus' birthplace and missed Jesus. Arguments about the details can be good and honest. But they can also become a way of keeping him at a distance. Whatever question you are carrying, keep asking it close to him.

passages.t: No one ever spoke like this man
passages.happening:
The officers come back without Jesus. The chief priests and Pharisees ask, “Why didn't you bring Him in?” (verse 45). The officers answer, “Never has anyone spoken like this man!” (verse 46).

The Pharisees are scornful. “Have you also been deceived?” they ask. “Have any of the rulers or Pharisees believed in Him? But this crowd that does not know the law, they are under a curse” (verses 47-49).

Then one of their own speaks up. Nicodemus, who came to Jesus at night in chapter 3, asks, “Does our law convict a man without first hearing from him to determine what he has done?” (verse 51). They turn on him. “Aren't you also from Galilee?” they reply. “Look into it, and you will see that no prophet comes out of Galilee” (verse 52).

Verse 53, “Then each went to his own home”, belongs with the story of the woman caught in adultery that follows (7:53 to 8:11). The oldest copies of John do not have that story, as John's book page explains. The notes on chapter 8 take it up.
passages.hearers:
The officers were probably the temple guard, sent by the chief priests. They went to arrest a man and came back having listened to him. Their excuse is not that he ran or that the crowd protected him. It is that no one had ever spoken like this.

The leaders' answer shows contempt for ordinary people: ‘this crowd that does not know the law’. They thought only the learned could judge rightly. John lets the irony stand. The crowd and the officers were listening, while the learned men were not.

Nicodemus asks only for fairness. He does not yet say he believes. He reminds the council of its own law: hear a man before you judge him. For that small act of courage he is mocked. We meet him once more at the end, when he brings spices to bury Jesus (19:39).

‘No prophet comes out of Galilee’ was not even accurate. The prophet Jonah came from Gath-hepher, a town in Galilee (2 Kings 14:25). Anger had made them careless with their own Scriptures.
passages.ot: The Law demanded fair hearings. Moses told Israel's judges, “Hear the disputes between your brothers, and judge fairly” (Deuteronomy 1:16), and, “Show no partiality in judging; hear both small and great alike” (Deuteronomy 1:17). Nicodemus appeals to that. And the Scriptures named a prophet from Galilee: “His servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher” (2 Kings 14:25).
passages.hard: Were the Pharisees all hostile to Jesus? Not here, and not everywhere. Nicodemus is a Pharisee and a ruler, and he defends a fair hearing. In chapter 19 he and Joseph of Arimathea, ‘a disciple of Jesus (but secretly for fear of the Jews)’, bury Jesus. The leaders in this scene speak for themselves, not for all Pharisees, and certainly not for all Jews. The crowd they despise is Jewish too, and many of them believe.
passages.asks: Nicodemus did not make a speech of faith. He asked for fairness, and it cost him the respect of his colleagues. Sometimes the first brave thing is small: asking that someone be heard before they are condemned. If you have been mocked for raising a fair question, Nicodemus has stood there before you. His story did not end in that room.
